section_1.title: Prerequisite: The Polarized Filter Analogy
section_1.content: Define light as an electromagnetic wave oscillating in all directions. Introduce polarizers as 'slotted fences' that restrict light to a single plane of oscillation.
section_1.example: Imagine a vertical picket fence allowing only vertical ropes to pass through. If you place a second fence horizontally, no rope gets through (the 'crossed polarizer' effect).

section_2.title: The Chirality of Sugar Molecules
section_2.content: Introduce the concept of optical activity. Molecules like sucrose are 'chiral'—they have a handedness. When light travels through a chiral solution, the electric field interacts with these molecules, causing the plane of polarization to rotate.
section_2.example: Visualize the sugar molecule as a spiral staircase. Light entering the liquid is forced to 'twist' its polarization plane as it interacts with these molecular spirals.

section_3.title: Mechanism: The Barber Pole Effect
section_3.content: Explain that different colors (wavelengths) of light rotate at different rates. If we use white light, the colors 'fanning out' create a gradient. As we change the concentration or the path length of the liquid, the light 'twists' further, appearing like a rotating barber pole.
section_3.example: Use a graphical animation: A beam of white light enters the beaker; as it travels deeper, the polarization vector traces a helix, mapping the 'candy-cane' stripe pattern onto the exit screen.

section_4.title: Quantitative Visualization: The Rotation Equation
section_4.content: Present the formula θ = [α] × c × l, where θ is the rotation angle. Use a visual graph where θ is the Y-axis and concentration (c) or length (l) is the X-axis, showing a linear growth of the twist.
section_4.example: A 'Sugar Meter' device where an animation of a dial moves clockwise as you slide a slider increasing the concentration of sugar in the tank.

section_5.title: Real-World Application: The Saccharimeter
section_5.content: Summarize how this effect is used in the food industry to measure sugar purity. By observing the degree of rotation, we can determine the exact concentration without touching the substance.
section_5.example: A quality control robot at a candy factory using a laser and polarized sensors to instantly detect the sugar density in a syrup vat, ensuring the 'sweetness' matches the recipe.

        lecture_lines = [
            "Different light wavelengths rotate at different rates.",
            "White light fans out creating color gradients.",
            "Deeper travel maps a candy-cane helical twist.",
            "Increasing path length makes the twist distinct.",
            "The effect resembles a rotating barber pole."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("Mechanism: The Barber Pole Effect", lecture_lines)

        # Animation Elements
